claims.text: A framework integrating Debye models, DFT vibrational spectra, and MD phonon-scattering simulations can accurately identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
Combining these simulation methods captures the complex scattering and vibrational mechanisms inherent to high-entropy alloys more effectively than existing approaches.
High-entropy alloys relevant to thermal insulation are typically disordered in their as-synthesized state.
Such alloys have multicomponent compositions and complex microstructures.
DFT can be used to compute phonon dispersion and soft-mode effects in these alloys.
MD simulations can model finite-temperature phonon scattering in these alloys.
Realistic interatomic potentials can be validated for high-entropy alloy systems.
Accurate modeling of phonon scattering in disordered atomic arrangements links alloy microstructure to effective phonon thermal conductivity.
Accurate modeling of vibrational density of states links alloy microstructure to effective phonon thermal conductivity.
Explicitly accounting for multiple phonon-scattering events produces a more realistic calculation of phonon transport.
Explicitly accounting for anharmonic interactions produces a more realistic calculation of phonon transport.
Capturing multiple scattering and anharmonic interactions reduces conductivity-prediction error relative to empirical or simplified models.
The proposed framework will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 15–30% over conventional methods.
The improvement will make identification of low-phonon-thermal-conductivity materials more reliable.
Current predictive methods rely largely on simplified semi-empirical or Debye-only approaches.
Current simplified approaches inadequately capture the full complexity of phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
The predicted improvement applies to high-entropy alloys having moderate disorder and compositional variation.
The approach may be less effective for alloys with extreme disorder.
The approach may be less effective when significant non-phononic conduction channels are present.
The approach may be less effective when interatomic potentials are poorly parameterized.
